titleEn: Winter Snowmobile Crash - Trauma Complicated by Moderate Hypothermia

patient.name: Tyler Banks
patient.affectEn: confused and drowsy; mumbling; opens his eyes when spoken to; tries to pull away when touched; minimizes his pain and keeps trying to sit up; cold, pale and waxy and NOT shivering; still in wet snowmobile gear
patient.speechEn: slurred, slow speech; gives confused answers and gives up halfway through sentences; most of the history has to come from his friends

scene.settingEn: Highway pullout off Highway 5 near Merritt, 1905 hrs in January. Snow-packed and icy, full dark, light snow, minus 12 degrees C with a light wind. Fire has set up scene lighting and closed the shoulder lane; a plough truck passes intermittently. Your ambulance is staged at the pullout. Search and Rescue arrive with the patient strapped in a rescue toboggan, still in wet snowmobile gear, wrapped in a foil blanket over the wet clothing. One patient. His two friends are with SAR and can give the history. Royal Inland Hospital (trauma centre) in Kamloops is 55 minutes by ground; air ambulance is unavailable due to weather.
hazardsEn: ice and snow-packed ground - slip hazard
traffic on the highway shoulder (shoulder lane closed by fire) and a plough truck passing intermittently
darkness - fire has set up scene lighting
cold (minus 12 degrees C, light wind) - to the crew as well as the patient

bystanders.knowsEn: He was riding a groomed trail at roughly 50 km/h when his snowmobile hit a stump buried under fresh snow; he went over the handlebars and landed on his left side about 8 metres away. Helmet on; the helmet is not damaged. They were riding ahead and did not see the crash itself. They came back about 45 minutes later and found him lying in the snow, awake but confused, with one leg obviously bent; the crash was at about 1800 this evening. Earlier he had gone through the slushy edge of a creek, so his snow pants and gloves were already soaked. They covered him with one jacket and rode out to a spot with cell service to call. He is healthy, takes no medications and has no known allergies. He ate a burger and had two beers at 1500 this afternoon. They do not know whether he was knocked out.

They carried him out in the rescue toboggan, still in his wet gear with a foil blanket over the wet clothing. He has been mumbling and confused the whole way and has not been shivering. The SAR team and fire can help with the lift, the scoop transfer, the helmet removal and equipment - only when told exactly what to do.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: ambulance patient compartment with heater (can be preheated to 30 degrees C)
spinal device with head blocks and body straps
padded board splints and triangular bandages
PCP only: IV start kit, normal saline, TXA

dispatchEn: 1905 hrs, January. Code 3 to a forest service road off Highway 5 near Merritt. A snowmobile has struck a buried stump and the rider was thrown. His two friends found him about 45 minutes after the crash and rode out to a spot with cell service to call. Air temperature minus 12 degrees C, light snow, full dark. Search and Rescue will bring the patient to the highway pullout by rescue toboggan; fire is staging with you at the pullout. Royal Inland Hospital in Kamloops is 55 minutes by ground and air ambulance is unavailable due to weather.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: the friends report the rider is awake but 'not making sense', his clothing is wet because he went through the slushy edge of a creek, and he was lying in the snow the whole time. They have covered him with one jacket. SAR estimates 10 minutes to reach you at the pullout.
arrivalEn: You are staged at the highway pullout with fire: snow-packed and icy, dark, minus 12 degrees C with a light wind. Fire has scene lighting up and the shoulder lane closed; a plough truck passes now and then. Search and Rescue come down the trail and bring the patient to you strapped in a rescue toboggan, still in wet snowmobile gear with a foil blanket wrapped over the wet clothing. One patient. His two friends are with SAR.
firstLookEn: A young adult male strapped in a rescue toboggan, helmet still on, wearing wet snowmobile gear under a foil blanket. He is moving his head and mumbling and looks confused. His skin is pale. He is NOT shivering.

primary.locEn: Opens his eyes to your voice, mumbles, gives confused answers and tries to pull away when touched. Altered level of consciousness (responds to voice).
primary.airwayEn: Clear, no blood or vomit - but he is drowsy and slow to protect it.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 12, slow and shallow. Equal air entry; tender on the left side of the chest.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse: none palpable at either wrist. Carotid: 48, weak and regular - found only on a prolonged check. If the candidate states a carotid check of 30 to 45 seconds (or a full 30 seconds or longer), give 48, weak and regular. If they state a check of 10 seconds or less, say only: 'You don't feel a pulse in that time.' If they give no duration, ask: 'How long are you checking for?' No external hemorrhage.
primary.rbsEn: Helmet on and intact, no head wound visible. Neck: cannot be cleared - he is confused. Chest: tender on the left, equal air entry. Abdomen: soft. Pelvis: stable. Left lower leg: obvious closed deformity with the boot still on; the foot is cool - but both feet are cold, so it has to be compared with the uninjured side. No external hemorrhage. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: cold, pale and waxy, no shivering.

history.ccEn: My leg... my leg hurts. And my side... I'm okay... I'm fine...

opqrst.oEn: I hit... something under the snow... went over the bars... (The friends: about 1800; a stump buried under fresh snow at roughly 50 km/h; he landed on his left side about 8 metres away.)
opqrst.pEn: Moving it... moving it's bad. Nothing helps.
opqrst.rEn: No... it's just my leg... and my side.
opqrst.sEn: Leg's a... 7, maybe. Ribs... 5. It's not that bad.
opqrst.tEn: Since I came off... I don't know how long. (The friends: the crash was about 45 minutes before they found him; he was lying in the snow the whole time.)

history.painScoreEn: Left lower leg 7 out of 10, left ribs 5 out of 10 - he minimizes it and keeps trying to sit up (a hypothermic, confused patient under-reports pain)

sample.sEn: My leg... my ribs... I'm cold... I want to sit up.
sample.aEn: No... none. (The friends: no known allergies.)
sample.pEn: I'm healthy... (The friends: healthy, no medical history.)
sample.lEn: A burger... couple of beers... around 3. (The friends: a burger and two beers at 1500 this afternoon.)
sample.eEn: Riding... went through the creek earlier, I was wet... then I hit something. (The friends: his snow pants and gloves were soaked from going through the slushy edge of a creek before the crash; he lay in the snow about 45 minutes before they found him; they covered him with one jacket.)

fe.generalEn: I'm fit... I ride every weekend. Haven't been sick.
fe.cnsEn: I don't... remember it clearly. My hands... they don't work. My legs aren't weak... I don't think.
fe.respiratoryEn: Hurts on the left... when I breathe in.
fe.giGuEn: I feel sick... I haven't thrown up. I haven't peed.
fe.integumentaryEn: My fingers and toes... they're white... numb. No blisters.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: My left leg... the lower part.
fe.eentEn: My eyes are fine... the visor was down.

findings.headNeckEn: Examined during a two-rescuer helmet removal with in-line stabilization: no scalp wound, no blood from the ears. Collar applied after the neck is inspected.
findings.chestLungsEn: Left lateral tenderness over ribs 8 to 10. Equal air entry at all six sites. No flail segment, no crepitus.
findings.backEn: Checked during the scoop transfer: no step deformity; the clothing underneath him is soaked through to the skin.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Closed mid-shaft tibia-fibula deformity on the left. With the boot removed carefully: the left foot is pale and cold with a weak but present dorsalis pedis pulse that is the same as the uninjured side; sensation reduced in both feet.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: Fingers white and hard to the touch with reduced sensation, no blisters, in both hands. Circulation and movement otherwise intact; no deformity.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: baseline, in the heated ambulance (BP difficult to auscultate over road noise - palpation acceptable if the candidate says so; pulse is carotid, radial not palpable; SpO2 will not read)

pulse.strength: weak, at the carotid; radial not palpable
pulse.rawEn: 48 weak regular at the carotid, radial not palpable

vitalsSets.skin: cold, pale and waxy; not shivering
vitalsSets.spo2: unobtainable - the probe will not pick up a reading on his cold fingers

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: improving with rewarming: only after the wet clothing is off AND active rewarming has started, from 20 minutes into the call (the scenario scripts it 30 minutes into the transport). Without rewarming, set 1 values persist.

pulse.strength: stronger - now palpable at the radial

vitalsSets.skin: cold but no longer waxy; shivering has restarted

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge and prepare the ambulance before the patient arrives: heat the patient compartment to 30 degrees C, lay out dry blankets, warm packs and towels, and have the scoop, collar, splints and shears ready
triggers: have the scoop and collar ready

expected.actionEn: Anticipate a combined problem: this is a trauma patient AND an environmental patient, and both have to be managed at once - hypothermia will not wait until the fractures are splinted
Plan for a long transport with no air option: confirm the destination, tell dispatch the ground ETA and ask whether a PCP or ALS intercept can meet you en route

Verbalize hazards (ice, traffic on the shoulder, plough truck, darkness, cold to the crew), environment (minus 12 C, dark, wind), MOI (snowmobile versus buried stump at speed, rider thrown, 45 minutes lying in snow) and people (one patient plus witnesses)
Don gloves and eye protection plus cold-weather and high-visibility gear; get the patient into the heated ambulance before doing anything you can do inside instead of outside
triggers: get him into the heated ambulance

expected.actionEn: First look: young adult male, wet clothing, mumbling and confused, NOT shivering - the absence of shivering in a cold patient means the hypothermia is no longer mild
Assess LOC / AVPU: responds to voice, confused - an altered LOC in a cold patient is a hypothermia sign, not just a head injury sign
triggers: do you know where you are

expected.actionEn: Manual in-line c-spine control and keep it: a thrown rider who is confused cannot be cleared by NEXUS, so spinal precautions stay on
Assess the airway; keep suction ready because a cold confused patient protects his airway poorly and may vomit
Assess breathing: recognize a slow shallow rate of 12 as inadequate ventilation, give oxygen and assist ventilations gently with a BVM without hyperventilating the cold heart
triggers: rate and depth of his breathing

expected.actionEn: Assess circulation taking a full 30 to 45 seconds to determine pulselessness in a severely cold patient - do not declare arrest on a 10 second check
Rapid body survey with the wet clothing cut away in the heated compartment, then immediately re-covered - expose in sections, never strip and leave him uncovered
Note the skin: cold, pale and waxy with no shivering, and say what that means - shivering stops below roughly 32 degrees, so this is at least moderate hypothermia
triggers: skin is cold pale and waxy

expected.actionEn: High-flow oxygen; the pulse oximeter is unreliable on cold peripheries so treat on clinical grounds rather than waiting for a number
Position supine, flat and still on a scoop; avoid any rough handling, jolting or unnecessary movement, which can trigger ventricular fibrillation in a cold heart
Categorize as RTC and state all four reasons: altered LOC, bradycardia with poor perfusion, hypothermia and the mechanism
Ready to load within 15 minutes while still handling him gently - one careful scoop transfer rather than several moves
Use SAR and fire personnel for the lift and for equipment so that your hands stay on the patient's airway and c-spine
Establish the chief complaint: leg and chest pain with confusion after a snowmobile crash and prolonged cold exposure

HxC/C using collateral history from the friends, covering speed, what he struck, distance thrown, landing position, helmet, LOC, AND the environmental history: how long down, wet clothing, wind exposure, any alcohol
triggers: how long was he lying in the snow

expected.actionEn: Pain score for each complaint, recognizing that a hypothermic confused patient under-reports pain
Past medical history from the friends
Medications
Allergies
Last oral intake, including the alcohol - it worsens heat loss and clouds the mental status picture
GCS with all three components
Blood pressure - state the method used and why, since auscultation is unreliable in a cold vasoconstricted patient in a noisy compartment
Pulse taken centrally over a full 30 to 45 seconds, with rate, rhythm and quality reported
Respiratory rate, depth and character, recognizing 12 and shallow as inadequate in this patient
Skin assessed hands-on - cold, waxy, no shivering
Pupils - sluggish reaction is consistent with hypothermia as well as head injury
SpO2 attempted and documented as unobtainable, with the reason given
Blood glucose - mandatory here because the LOC is decreased and hypoglycaemia both mimics and worsens hypothermia
Temperature - this is the vital sign that decides the treatment path, so measure it and repeat it
FE - General health
FE - CNS (confusion here has two possible causes, head injury and hypothermia, and both must be reported)
FE - Respiratory
FE - Cardiovascular
FE - GI/GU
FE - Integumentary (white numb digits raise local cold injury on top of the systemic hypothermia)
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT
Head and neck examined during a controlled two-rescuer helmet removal with in-line stabilization maintained
triggers: remove the helmet with in-line stabilization

expected.actionEn: Chest examined with six-site auscultation
Abdomen examined
Back examined during the scoop transfer and the wet clothing removed from underneath him, not just from the front
Upper extremities examined for local cold injury as well as trauma, comparing both hands
Lower extremities with the deformity documented and the distal pulse compared against the uninjured limb, because every extremity is cold in this patient
Remove ALL wet clothing by cutting, dry the skin, and wrap in dry blankets inside the heated compartment before anything else that can wait
triggers: cut off all the wet clothes

expected.actionEn: Actively rewarm for moderate hypothermia: ambulance heated to 30 degrees C, warm blankets, and hot packs wrapped in towels applied to the trunk only - never directly on skin and never on the extremities
Handle him gently throughout: one transfer, no jolting, no rubbing or massaging cold limbs, no sitting him up - rough handling can precipitate ventricular fibrillation in a cold heart
Two-rescuer helmet removal with in-line stabilization, hard collar and a single scoop transfer onto the spinal device
Splint the left tib-fib immobilizing the joints above and below, with distal circulation, sensation and movement compared against the uninjured leg before and after
triggers: compare CSM with the other leg

expected.actionEn: Give oxygen and assist ventilations gently with a BVM; do not hyperventilate and do not give anything by mouth to a confused hypothermic patient
Verbalize that all analgesia is withheld and why: Entonox and methoxyflurane are contraindicated by the altered LOC, and oral drugs are unsafe in a confused patient
Reassess ABCs and all interventions after each move and at least every 5 minutes
Repeat the temperature and report the rewarming trend, not just a single number
Second full set of vitals within 5-6 minutes of the first for a priority patient, then repeated through the long transport
Recheck distal circulation, sensation and movement below the splint against the uninjured leg after every move
State the hypothermic arrest plan: CPR, AED analyze, up to three shocks if indicated, then continue CPR without pausing to analyze again, and keep transporting
Early notification to the receiving trauma centre with the core temperature included
Complete hand-off covering both the trauma and the environmental picture, including the rewarming timeline
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes, documenting temperatures, the pulse check duration and the rewarming measures

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate (or a helper on the candidate's instruction) cuts off or removes the patient's wet clothing and dries him (good act; also detected from the candidate's words)
candidate starts active rewarming: hot packs wrapped in towels to the trunk, warm blankets, or the patient compartment heated to 30 degrees C (good act; also detected from the candidate's words)
candidate puts hot packs directly on the skin without a towel or wrap, or applies them to the arms, legs, hands or feet instead of the trunk (armpits, chest, groin)
candidate rubs or massages his limbs to warm them, sits him up or lets him sit up, lets him walk or do any activity, or jolts him or moves him roughly or repeatedly when one careful transfer would do

candidate starts chest compressions, or declares cardiac arrest and runs the AED arrest sequence, while the patient has a pulse (carotid 48) - e.g. after a radial check or a carotid check of 10 seconds or less. Stating what they would do IF he arrests is NOT this event.

the helmet is removed while nobody is holding manual in-line stabilization of the head and neck, or by a single rescuer, or pulled off without supporting the neck; a two-rescuer removal with one person maintaining in-line stabilization throughout is correct

candidate (or the partner on the candidate's instruction) lets go of manual c-spine control before the patient is secured on the scoop / spinal device with head blocks and straps; applying the collar alone does not permit release. Handing manual control directly to another rescuer without a gap is NOT a release.

candidate moves the patient, asks him to lift or turn his head or sit up, or applies a pain stimulus before manual in-line c-spine control has been established. SAR carrying him to the pullout before the crew took over is NOT this event.
candidate tapes the patient's head to the spinal device
candidate ventilates with the BVM at a deliberately fast rate or forcefully, instead of gentle assisted ventilation
candidate gives the patient anything to eat or drink by mouth (e.g. warm drinks)
PCP runs a saline bolus past 500 mL, or onto the next 500 mL, without reassessing the patient (BP / vitals / ABCs) in between

drugs.doseEn: self-administered by inhalation - WITHHELD in this scenario: contraindicated by the altered level of consciousness
3 mL self-administered via inhaler - WITHHELD in this scenario: contraindicated by the decreased level of consciousness (and a possible head injury)
500 - 1,000 mg PO - WITHHELD in this scenario: nothing by mouth to a confused hypothermic patient
300-400 mg PO - WITHHELD in this scenario: nothing by mouth to a confused hypothermic patient
15 g PO - NOT indicated: BGL 4.4 mmol/L is not below 4.0, and he cannot reliably protect his airway
0.5 - 1 mg IM or 3 mg IN for hypoglycemia - NOT indicated: BGL 4.4 mmol/L is not below 4.0
PCP only: vascular access with warmed fluid if hypotension persists after rewarming begins; any bolus 20 mL/kg to a maximum of 2 litres, reassessing every 500 mL
2 g (2000 mg) IV push over 1 minute - NOT indicated in this scenario: no signs of shock from blood loss (the bradycardia and low pressure are from the hypothermia)

notificationFacts.hxcc: unwitnessed crash, found confused; leg pain 7/10 and rib pain 5/10, under-reported; two beers at 1500
notificationFacts.vitals: tympanic 30.5 C (moderate hypothermia), GCS 13, carotid 48 weak with no radial pulse on a 45 second check, resp 12 shallow, BP 96/62 by palpation, SpO2 unobtainable, BGL 4.4; latest GCS 14, BP 104/68, pulse 58 radial palpable, resp 14, SpO2 95% on 15 L, temperature 31.4 C, shivering again

notificationFacts.findings: closed left mid-shaft tib-fib deformity with distal pulse equal to the uninjured side; left lateral rib tenderness with equal air entry; white numb fingers and toes

handoffFacts.cc: left lower leg pain 7/10 and left rib pain 5/10, with confusion
handoffFacts.moi: struck a buried stump at roughly 50 km/h at about 1800, went over the handlebars and landed on his left side about 8 metres away; helmeted, no helmet damage; unwitnessed
handoffFacts.hxcc: lay in the snow about 45 minutes before his friends found him, clothing already soaked from going through a creek edge; confused since found; under-reports his pain; two beers at 1500
handoffFacts.initialVitals: not shivering, tympanic 30.5 C, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), no palpable radial pulse, carotid 48 weak and regular found over a 45 second check, resp 12 shallow, BP 96/62 by palpation, skin cold pale and waxy, pupils equal and sluggish, SpO2 unobtainable, BGL 4.4 mmol/L
handoffFacts.finalVitals: GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6), BP 104/68, pulse 58 stronger and now palpable at the radial, resp 14, skin cold but no longer waxy with shivering restarted, pupils equal with improving reaction, SpO2 95% on 15 L, BGL 4.6 mmol/L, temperature 31.4 C tympanic
handoffFacts.treatments: two-rescuer helmet removal with in-line stabilization, hard collar, single scoop transfer onto the spinal device; all wet clothing cut off and skin dried (time documented), dry blankets, compartment at 30 degrees C, hot packs wrapped in towels to the trunk only, no rubbing or massage; oxygen 15 L with gentle BVM-assisted ventilation, no hyperventilation; left tib-fib splinted with distal CSM compared to the uninjured leg before and after; gentle handling throughout; no analgesia - Entonox and methoxyflurane contraindicated by the altered LOC, nothing by mouth; last oral intake a burger and two beers at 1500
handoffFacts.findings: moderate hypothermia 30.5 C rising to 31.4 C; bradycardia 48 rising to 58; GCS 13 improving to 14; closed left mid-shaft tib-fib deformity with a weak dorsalis pedis pulse equal to the uninjured side; left lateral rib tenderness over ribs 8 to 10 with equal air entry; white numb fingers and toes with no blistering (local cold injury)

examinerPrompts.locNotDepictedEn: He mumbles, opens his eyes when you speak to him and gives confused answers; he tries to pull away when he is touched.
examinerPrompts.breathingNotDepictedEn: His breathing is slow and shallow.
examinerPrompts.missedInjuryEn: You assessed his chest and his legs during your rapid body survey - what did you find there?

trackNotes.emrEn: This whole call sits inside EMR scope and that is the point: removing wet clothing, drying, insulating, heating the compartment to 30 degrees, trunk-only wrapped hot packs, gentle handling, two-rescuer helmet removal, collar and scoop, a tib-fib splint with comparative CSM checks, oxygen and gentle BVM support, a 30 to 45 second pulse check, and readiness to run CPR with the AED using the hypothermic three-shock rule. All analgesia is withheld for altered LOC. What EMR cannot do here - warmed IV fluid, CPAP - is exactly what makes the mechanical basics decisive on a 55 minute transport.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds the 9-system Functional Enquiry, vascular access with warmed fluid if hypotension persists after rewarming begins, and closer airway management if the LOC falls further. PCP must still follow the same hypothermia rules: no active rewarming below 28 degrees, trunk-only heat packs, and a 30 to 45 second pulse check before declaring arrest.

sourcePages: Scenario etr-03 (data/practical/emr-trauma-1.json): dispatch, scene, primary (30-45 second pulse check), transport, history (collateral from friends), vitals sets 1-2, FE, exam, interventions (trauma and environmental in parallel, active rewarming for moderate hypothermia, analgesia withheld, EMR scope), ongoing (rewarming trend, hypothermic arrest plan), handoff, critical pitfalls. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (altered LOC, absent radial pulses); p.11 primary survey interventions (c-spine stabilization, airway suctioning with decreased LOC, assisting slow or shallow respirations with decreasing LOC, oxygen, gradual warming for hypothermia); p.12 critical history questions; p.21 Musculoskeletal Injuries (joints above and below, distal pulses); p.25 Spinal Management (do not tape the head); p.29 Hypothermia (30-45 seconds to determine pulselessness; remove wet and cold clothing and cover; take temperature; in arrest AED and up to three defibrillations then CPR without pausing; moderate 28-32 C actively rewarm - preheat the ambulance to 30 C, hot packs wrapped in towels, warm blankets; severe < 28 C do not actively rewarm, avoid rough handling); p.54 Hypovolemia (PCP bolus 20 mL/kg to a maximum of 2 L, reassessing every 500 mL); p.57 Diabetic Emergencies (BGL < 4.0 mmol/L for glucose gel / glucagon); p.58 Acetaminophen; p.65 Entonox (contraindicated: altered LOC); p.67 Glucagon; p.68 Ibuprofen; p.71 Methoxyflurane (contraindicated: decreased LOC or head injury); p.76 Oral Glucose (15 g PO; sufficient mentation to maintain an airway); p.78 Tranexamic Acid (indications). EMALB Practical Grading Criteria p.35 (priority vitals: 7-8 minutes between sets = moderate delay, > 9 minutes = major) and p.36 (chest compressions on a patient with a pulse).
